title: Cyber Crime and Cyber Law
part: Part B — Cyber Safety and E-Commerce

blocks.html: After studying this chapter you will be able to:

items.html: define cyberspace, cyber crime and cyber law
classify cyber crimes by their target
describe common cyber crimes such as hacking, phishing, identity theft, cyberstalking, DoS attacks and online fraud
explain the main provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and other Indian laws
protect yourself from cyber crime and report it correctly

blocks.html: Cyberspace is the virtual world created by computers, networks and the internet, where people communicate, shop, study, bank and play. Like any crowded place, it also attracts criminals.
Definition: A cyber crime is any illegal act in which a computer, mobile phone or network is used as a tool (e.g. to cheat someone) or is the target (e.g. hacking into a server).

items.html: Hundreds of millions of new internet users, many unaware of risks.
Money and personal data are now online (UPI, net banking, Aadhaar-linked services).
Criminals can act from far away and hide their identity.
Easy availability of hacking tools and stolen data.

rows: Cyberstalking, cyberbullying, identity theft, phishing, email spoofing, online defamation
Credit card and UPI fraud, software piracy, theft of data, intellectual property violation
Hacking of company servers, DoS attacks, ransomware, data breaches
Cyber terrorism, attacks on power grids or banking systems, spreading fake news that causes violence

blocks.html: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer or network. A black-hat hacker does it to steal or damage. An ethical (white-hat) hacker is hired by a company to find weaknesses so they can be fixed — this is legal because it is done with permission.

Phishing uses fake emails, messages or websites that look like they come from a bank, a delivery company, a government scheme or a popular app, to trick people into giving passwords, card numbers or OTPs.

items.html: Vishing — phishing by voice call ("I am calling from your bank").
Smishing — phishing by SMS ("Your electricity will be cut tonight, call this number").

blocks.caption: Figure 6.1 · How a phishing attack works and where to stop it

blocks.html: Stealing someone's personal details (name, Aadhaar, PAN, photos, passwords) to pretend to be them — for example, opening a fake social media profile or taking a loan in their name.

items.html: Card and UPI fraud — tricking victims into sharing OTP or PIN, or into scanning a QR code to "receive" money (scanning a QR code with a PIN always sends money).
SIM swap — getting a duplicate SIM of the victim's number to receive their OTPs.
Lottery, prize and job scams — "You have won ₹25 lakh, pay a processing fee."
Fake loan and investment apps — promise easy loans or high returns, then steal data or harass.
Fake customer care numbers placed online.
Cyberstalking — repeatedly following, watching or threatening a person online.
Cyberbullying — insulting, humiliating, threatening or excluding someone through messages, posts or comments. It harms mental health and can be a crime.

blocks.html: Pretending to be someone else electronically: email spoofing (a forged sender address), caller-ID spoofing, website spoofing (a copy of a real site at a slightly different address such as sbi-onlinee.com).

A DoS attack floods a website or server with so many fake requests that genuine users cannot use it. In a Distributed DoS (DDoS) attack, thousands of infected computers (a botnet) attack together. Targets include banking, ticket-booking and government websites.
Viruses, worms, trojans and spyware damage systems or steal data (Chapter 13). Ransomware locks files and demands payment to unlock them.

items.html: Data theft and data breaches — stealing customer databases.
Software piracy — copying or selling software illegally.
Cyber defamation — posting false statements that damage someone's reputation.
Publishing or sharing obscene content — a serious offence.
Cyber terrorism — attacks on critical infrastructure to threaten the nation.
Spreading fake news and rumours that cause panic or violence.

blocks.html: Cyber law is the part of law that deals with the internet, computers, electronic records and cyber crime. It is needed because ordinary laws were written for a world of paper documents and physical theft.
India's main cyber law is the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000, which came into force on 17 October 2000. It was strengthened by the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008.

items.html: Give legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, so that contracts and documents can be online.
Support e-governance and e-commerce.
Define cyber crimes and their penalties.
Set up authorities: the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) for digital signatures and CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) for responding to cyber security incidents.

rows: Damage to a computer or data without permission (e.g. copying data, introducing viruses) — compensation to the victim
Computer-related offences, including hacking with dishonest intent
Identity theft — misusing someone's password, digital signature or other unique identity
Cheating by personation using a computer (e.g. pretending to be a bank officer online)
Violation of privacy — capturing or publishing private images without consent
Publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically
Breach of confidentiality and privacy by a person with lawful access

blocks.html: Note: Section 66A, which punished "offensive" online messages, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 (Shreya Singhal v. Union of India) because it was too vague and restricted freedom of speech.

items.html: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code) — covers cheating, defamation, criminal intimidation and other offences, including when they are committed online.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — protects personal data and sets duties for organisations that collect it.
Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) — under the Ministry of Home Affairs; runs the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) and the helpline 1930.
Cyber cells in state police departments investigate cyber crimes.

blocks.html: A digital signature is an electronic, encrypted signature that proves who signed a document and that it was not changed afterwards. Under the IT Act it is as valid as a handwritten signature. Digital Signature Certificates are issued by Certifying Authorities licensed by the CCA. Aadhaar-based e-Sign lets citizens sign documents online.

items.html: Use strong, unique passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.
Never share OTP, PIN, CVV or passwords — not with anyone, not even "bank officials".
Check website addresses carefully and look for https.
Download apps only from official app stores; check permissions.
Keep the operating system, apps and antivirus updated.
Do not click unknown links or open unexpected attachments.
Keep social media profiles private; do not post your address, phone number or travel

blocks.html: plans publicly.

items.html: Do not accept friend requests from strangers or meet online contacts in person

blocks.html: without your parents.

items.html: Verify news before forwarding it.

blocks.html: 10. Back up important data regularly.

items.html: Money fraud: call 1930 immediately — quick reporting can freeze the money before the criminal withdraws it. Inform your bank and block cards/UPI.
Other cyber crimes: report on cybercrime.gov.in or at the nearest police station or cyber cell.
Keep evidence: screenshots, messages, transaction IDs, phone numbers, URLs. Do not delete chats.
Tell a trusted adult (parent or teacher) at once if you are bullied, threatened or blackmailed online. It is never your fault, and help is available.

blocks.html: Did you know? CERT-In, set up in 2004, is India's national agency for responding to cyber security incidents. Organisations must report certain cyber incidents to it within six hours.
Aim: To recognise cyber crimes and practise safe habits.

items.html: Spot the fraud. Your teacher will display 10 messages (bank alerts, prize offers, delivery notices, school circulars). Classify each as genuine or fraudulent and list the red flags.
Check a URL. For five website addresses given by your teacher, decide whether each is genuine, and explain how you decided (spelling, domain, https).
Password health check. List the types of accounts you and your family use. For each, note whether the password is unique and whether 2FA is turned on (do not write actual passwords).
Privacy settings. With a parent, review the privacy settings of one social media or messaging app and make the profile private.
Explore the reporting portal. Visit cybercrime.gov.in and note the categories under which crimes can be reported. Do not file a test complaint.
Role play. In pairs, act out a vishing call from a fake "bank officer" and show the correct way to respond.
Cyber crime is any crime in which a computer or network is a tool or a target; it can be against individuals, property, organisations or the nation.

Common cyber crimes: hacking, phishing (vishing, smishing), identity theft, UPI and card fraud, SIM swap, cyberstalking, cyberbullying, spoofing, DoS/DDoS, malware, ransomware, piracy, defamation and cyber terrorism.
The IT Act, 2000 (amended 2008) recognises electronic records and digital signatures and defines cyber offences in sections 43, 65, 66, 66C, 66D, 66E, 66F, 67 and 72.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the DPDP Act, 2023 also apply; CERT-In and I4C are key agencies.
Report financial fraud on 1930 and other cyber crimes on cybercrime.gov.in, and keep all evidence.
